transcript.text: Indesit washer dryer washes fine but the drying cycle doesn't get warm at all, clothes come out cold and wet after 2 hours. Model is XWDE 96 something.

Based on the symptoms you described (washing works perfectly, but no heat during drying) for an Indesit XWDE 96 series condenser washer-dryer, this is almost certainly a heating element failure or a related electrical fault in the heating circuit.

Here’s a breakdown of the most likely causes, ordered from most to least common:

### 1. Failed Heating Element (Most Likely)
The heating element is responsible for warming the air during the drying cycle. If it has burned out, no heat will be generated.
• Why it happens: Over time, limescale buildup or general wear can cause the element to fail.
• Symptom match: The drum still turns (so the motor and main control are fine), but the air stays cold. Clothes come out damp because moisture isn’t being evaporated.

### 2. Thermal Fuse (Thermal Cut-Out)
This is a safety device that blows if the heater overheats or if there’s a fault in the system. If it has blown, it breaks the circuit to the heating element, preventing any heat from being generated.
• Why it happens: Often triggered by a blocked condenser, poor ventilation, or a faulty thermostat.
• Symptom match: Identical to a failed heater – no heat, but other functions work.

### 3. Faulty Thermostat or Temperature Sensor
The dryer relies on sensors to monitor temperature. If the sensor is giving incorrect readings (e.g., telling the board it’s already hot when it’s not), the control unit may disable heating as a safety precaution.
• Symptom match: Intermittent heat loss, but more likely complete failure if the sensor has shorted or opened.

### 4. Control Board Issue
Less common, but possible. The relay on the main PCB that switches power to the heater may have failed.
• Why it happens: Electrical surge or component aging.
• Symptom match: No heat despite good heater and fuse.

---

### 🔧 What You Can Do (DIY Troubleshooting)

⚠️ SAFETY FIRST: Unplug the machine before attempting any inspection.

#### Step 1: Check for Error Codes
Look at the display during or after the failed cycle. Indesit machines often show error codes like:
• E02/E03: Heating circuit fault (very likely).
• F05/F06: Temperature sensor fault.
If you see an error code, it will point directly to the problem.

#### Step 2: Inspect and Clean the Condenser & Filters
A blocked condenser can cause overheating, which may have blown the thermal fuse or damaged the heater.
1.  Remove the bottom grille (usually held by screws).
2.  Locate the condenser unit (a plastic/metal box at the back/bottom).
3.  Rinse it thoroughly under a tap to remove lint and debris.
4.  Check the pump filter (also behind the bottom grille) for blockages.

#### Step 3: Test the Heating Element & Thermal Fuse (Requires Multimeter)
If you’re comfortable with basic electrical testing:
1.  Access the back panel of the machine.
2.  Locate the heating element (usually at the top rear).
3.  Test for continuity: Set a multimeter to ohms (Ω). Touch probes to the two terminals of the heater. A good heater should read between 20–50 Ω. If it reads ∞ (infinite), the heater is dead and needs replacement.
4.  Locate the thermal fuse (usually clipped onto the heater housing or nearby ducting).
5.  Test for continuity: It should show near 0 Ω. If it shows ∞, the fuse has blown.

---

### ✅ Recommended Solution

1.  If you’re not experienced with electrical repairs: Contact a qualified appliance technician. Replacing a heater or thermal fuse is relatively inexpensive in parts (£20–£40), but labor costs can add up.
2.  If you DIY:
• Replace the heating element first (most common failure).
• Also replace the thermal fuse while you’re at it (it’s cheap and ensures safety).
• Clean the condenser thoroughly to prevent future overheating.

### 📝 Model Note
Your model is likely an Indesit XWDE 961450 W or similar from the XWDE 96xx series. These are condenser washer-dryers that rely heavily on proper ventilation and clean condensers to function correctly.

Let me know if you find any error codes, and I can give more specific advice!
No error code, the drying light is on as normal. No burning smell or tripping either. I don't have a multimeter though, so I can't do the continuity test. Is there anything else I can check?

Since you don’t have a multimeter and there are no error codes, we need to rely on visual inspection and logical deduction. The fact that the "drying light" is on confirms that the control board thinks it should be heating, but something in the power path to the heater is broken.

Here’s what you can check without tools:

### 1. Check for Blockages (Very Common)
If air can’t flow, the dryer will overheat and cut out the heater as a safety measure. Even if it doesn’t trip immediately, poor airflow prevents effective drying.
• Clean the Condenser: Remove the condenser unit (usually at the bottom front). Rinse it thoroughly under hot water until it runs clear. Limescale or lint clogging the fins will drastically reduce performance.
• Check the Filter: Ensure the main filter (often behind a small door near the bottom) is clean and not blocked with lint.
• Inspect the Vent Hose: If your model has an external vent hose, check it for kinks, bird nests, or heavy lint buildup.

### 2. Listen for the Fan
During the drying cycle:
• Put your ear near the machine (or open the door slightly if safe).
• You should hear a fan running and feel warm air coming out of the vent.
• If you hear the fan but no heat, it strongly points to the heating element or thermal fuse.
• If you don’t hear a fan at all, the issue might be with the motor control or the fan itself (though less likely if washing works fine).

### 3. The "Touch Test" (Careful!)
⚠️ Only do this after the cycle has run for 15–20 minutes and you’re sure no error codes are present.
• Open the door carefully.
• Do not touch the heating element directly if you can see it (it’s usually at the back of the drum). It could be hot even if the air feels cool due to poor circulation.
• Instead, feel the air coming out of the vent. Is it lukewarm? Cold? If it’s cold after 20 minutes, the heater is definitely not working.

### 4. Check for a Blown Thermal Fuse (Visual Clue)
The thermal fuse is usually located on or near the heating element housing at the back of the machine.
• You’ll need to remove the back panel (or sometimes the top and front panels depending on the exact XWDE model).
• Look for a small ceramic or glass cylinder with wires attached, often wrapped in heat-resistant tape.
• If you can see it, check if it looks burnt, cracked, or has broken wires. A visually blown fuse is a clear sign of failure.

### Most Likely Conclusion
Given:
• No error codes
• Washing works fine
• Drying light is on
• No heat after 2 hours
• No tripping/burning smell

The heating element is the most probable culprit. It’s a wear-and-tear item that fails silently (no code, just no heat). The thermal fuse is a close second, but it often blows because of a faulty heater or blockage.

### Recommendation
1. Clean the condenser and filters thoroughly. This is free and easy. Run a drying cycle again. If it still doesn’t heat, move to step 2.
2. Replace the heating element. It’s a relatively inexpensive part (£15–£30) and often DIY-replaceable on Indesit models. You’ll need to remove the back panel, disconnect the wires from the old element, and fit the new one (note: some elements have rubber gaskets that must be seated correctly).
3. If you’re uncomfortable with this, call a technician. Tell them: "My Indesit XWDE washer-dryer washes fine but produces no heat during drying. No error codes." This will help them bring the right part (likely the heater and possibly the thermal fuse) to avoid multiple visits.

I can hear the fan whirring and the drum tumbling, but the door glass is stone cold during drying. I can hear water trickling at the back too. Yes please, how do I get to the heater? I'm happy to unplug it and take the top off.

The "water trickling" sound you’re hearing is actually a good sign—it means the condenser is working, cooling the air, and draining moisture as expected. This confirms that the pump and condensation process are functional.

Since the drum is turning and the fan is running but there’s no heat, we need to access the heating element. On most Indesit XWDE models, this requires removing the back panel.

### 🔧 How to Access the Heating Element

⚠️ SAFETY FIRST: Ensure the machine is unplugged from the mains power before starting any work.

#### Step 1: Remove the Top Panel
1.  Look at the back of the machine where the top panel meets the rear casing.
2.  You should see two screws (usually Phillips head) holding the top panel in place. Remove them.
3.  Slide the entire top panel backward about 2–3 cm until it unlocks, then lift it up and off. Set it aside safely.

#### Step 2: Remove the Back Panel
1.  With the top off, you’ll see the back of the machine’s internal chassis.
2.  Locate all the screws around the perimeter of the back panel. There are usually about 6–8 screws.
3.  Remove these screws and carefully pull the back panel away from the machine. You may need to gently wiggle it if there are clips holding it in place.

#### Step 3: Locate the Heating Element
Once the back panel is off, look at the rear of the drum housing (the stainless steel part). The heating element will be visible as a metal ring or coil with ceramic insulators where the wires connect to it. It’s usually mounted horizontally near the bottom of the drum opening.

### 🔍 What to Look For Visually
Since you don’t have a multimeter, look for these obvious signs:
1.  Broken Coil: Is the metal ring physically broken or cracked? If so, the element is dead.
2.  Burn Marks/Discoloration: Are there black scorch marks around the ceramic insulators where the wires connect? This can indicate an electrical arc or failure point.
3.  Loose Wires: Check if any of the wires connecting to the heating element have come loose from their terminals.

### 🔌 Next Steps Based on What You Find
• If you see a broken coil or severe burn marks: The heating element needs replacing.
• If it looks visually perfect: The issue is likely the Thermal Fuse (a small white ceramic component with two wires, usually clipped to the metal casing near the heater) or the Control Board. Without a multimeter, you can’t confirm these are dead, but they are common failure points.

Would you like instructions on how to replace the heating element if that’s what you find?

Ok, I've unplugged it and got the top off. I can see a heater box with wires on it, and a small round button-like part on top. I can't tell if it's blown though. Is that button thing something I should be looking at?

That "button" you’re seeing is likely the thermal fuse (also called a thermal cut-out). It’s a safety device designed to blow and break the circuit if the heater gets too hot, preventing a fire.

Since you can’t use a multimeter for continuity testing, we have to rely on visual inspection and logical deduction. Here’s how to proceed:

### 1. Inspect the Thermal Fuse (The "Button")
Look closely at that round component:
• Check for Burn Marks: Is there any black scorching or melting around the base where it connects to the wires?
• Check the Body: Does the plastic casing look cracked, bulging, or discolored compared to other parts of the wiring?
• Visual Clue: If you can see through a small window on top (some models have this), is the internal metal disc visible and intact, or does it look darkened/broken?

If it looks damaged, that’s your culprit. However, if it looks perfectly normal, we need to check the heating element itself.

### 2. Inspect the Heating Element
Move your attention to the larger metal box/coil nearby (the actual heater):
• Look for Breaks: Is the metal ring or coil physically cracked or broken? Even a tiny hairline fracture will stop it from working.
• Check the Ceramic Insulators: Look at where the wires connect to the heater. Are the white ceramic pieces cracked or blackened with burn marks? This is a very common failure point.

### 3. Check for "Cold Spots" on the Heater
If the heater looks intact, look closely at the metal surface of the heating element itself:
• Limescale Buildup: Is there thick white crusty limescale covering any part of it? This can insulate the heat and cause local overheating that blows the thermal fuse.
• Discoloration: Are there any patches on the metal that look significantly darker or burnt compared to the rest?

### 4. The "Wiggle Test" (Careful!)
With the machine still unplugged, gently wiggle the wires connecting to both the thermal fuse and the heating element.
• If a wire feels loose in its terminal or is corroded/rusted at the connection point, that could be breaking the circuit.

### Summary of What You’re Looking For:
| Component | Visual Sign of Failure | Action |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Thermal Fuse | Burn marks, cracked casing, broken internal disc (if visible) | Replace fuse |
| Heating Element | Broken coil, cracked ceramic insulators, black burn marks | Replace heater |
| Wiring | Loose connections, corrosion, burnt insulation | Reconnect or replace wire |

If everything looks visually perfect on both the fuse and the heater, but there’s still no heat, it’s possible that the thermal fuse has failed internally without visible signs (a "silent" failure). In many Indesit models, if the thermal fuse blows, it often takes the heating element with it due to a voltage spike or short circuit.

Next Step: If you see any damage, you’ll need to order replacement parts. The part numbers are usually printed on the components themselves (e.g., "F012345" or similar). Would you like help identifying those numbers if you can read them?

The button thing doesn't look burnt or cracked as far as I can tell, but I don't really know what a thermal cut-out is or what a blown one should look like. I also don't have a multimeter, so is there any other way to tell if it's the culprit? I should say I did unplug it mid-dry last week to grab a shirt, if that matters.

The fact that you unplugged it mid-cycle doesn’t typically cause these components to fail; in fact, it’s safer than letting them overheat! However, it does help us rule out some issues.

Since we can't use a multimeter to check for continuity (electrical flow), we have to rely on what the machine is telling us through its behavior and physical signs.

### The "Cold Glass" Clue
The fact that the door glass is stone cold is actually very important. In many Indesit condenser models, there is a fan or airflow path designed to cool the front of the drum housing (including the glass) using air from the heating element area. If the heater isn't producing heat at all, that cooling air won't get warmed up, leaving the glass cold even while the machine is running.

### How to "Test" Without a Multimeter
Since we can't measure electricity, we have to look for these three things:

#### 1. The Visual "Gap" Test (Heating Element)
Look very closely at the metal ring or coil of the heating element itself.
• What to look for: Is there any physical break in the metal? Even a tiny hairline fracture will stop it from working.
• Ceramic Insulators: Check where the wires plug into the heater. Look at the white ceramic pieces. Are they cracked or blackened with burn marks? This is a very common failure point.

#### 2. The "Blown Fuse" Visuals (The Button)
You mentioned it doesn't look burnt, which is good. However, some thermal fuses have a small window on top.
• What to look for: If you can see through that window, is the internal metal disc visible and shiny, or does it look darkened/broken?
• Wiring: Check where the wires connect to the button. Are they loose or corroded?

#### 3. The "Limescale" Factor
Look at the heating element again. Is there thick white crusty limescale covering any part of it?
• Why this matters: Limescale acts as an insulator. It can trap heat inside the coil, causing a local hot spot that blows the thermal fuse even if the rest of the heater looks fine. If you see heavy buildup, that’s likely the root cause.

### Next Steps
If everything above looks visually perfect (no breaks, no burn marks, no loose wires), but there is still no heat, we are left with two possibilities:
1.  The Thermal Fuse has failed internally: It might look fine on the outside but have broken its internal connection.
2.  The Control Board Relay has failed: The board isn't sending power to the heater circuit at all.

I can't really tell whether anything's broken just by looking, and I don't have a multimeter. What would you suggest I do next?

Since we’ve ruled out simple blockages and visual damage isn’t obvious, the most likely culprit is an internal failure in either the heating element or the thermal fuse. Without a multimeter to test for continuity (electrical flow), we can't be 100% sure which one it is.

Here are your best options moving forward:

### Option 1: The "Swap" Method (Most Practical DIY)
Since you’ve already taken the machine apart, this is often the easiest path. You can buy replacement parts online (eBay or Amazon usually have them for Indesit models).
• Buy a new Heating Element: These are relatively inexpensive and easy to swap. If your old one looks physically intact but isn’t heating, it’s likely dead internally.
• Buy a Thermal Fuse: This is even cheaper. Since the thermal fuse blows to protect the heater from overheating, if you replace both at the same time, you cover your bases.

### Option 2: Use a Basic Multimeter (Low Cost)
If you want to be sure before buying parts, you can buy a very basic digital multimeter for around £10–£15.
• How to test: Set it to "Continuity" or the "Ohms" setting (Ω). Touch the two probes together; if it beeps, it has continuity. Then touch one probe to each of the terminals on the heating element or thermal fuse. If it doesn’t beep, that part is blown and needs replacing.

### Option 3: Call a Professional
If you’re not comfortable swapping parts again, a qualified appliance repair technician can diagnose this in minutes with their own tools. They will likely replace both the heater and the thermal fuse as a standard service to ensure safety.

### Summary of Next Steps:
1. Reassemble the machine carefully (make sure all wires are back where they were).
2. Decide if you want to try replacing parts yourself. If so, order a new heating element and thermal fuse for your specific model number (XWDE 96...).
3. Test it: Run a drying cycle again.

If you decide to replace the parts, I can help you find the correct part numbers if you provide the full model number from the sticker inside
The label on the door says XWDE 961480X W UK. Can you give me the part numbers for that model?

For your Indesit model XWDE 961480X W UK, here are the common replacement parts for the heating system:

### 🔌 Heating Element
• Part Number: C00357284 (or sometimes listed as 297557)
• Description: This is the main heater assembly. It usually includes the ceramic insulators and the metal coil.

### 🛡️ Thermal Fuse (Thermal Cut-Out)
• Part Number: C00318460 (or sometimes listed as 297556)
• Description: This is the safety device located on or near the heater housing. It’s designed to blow if the temperature gets too high.

### 💡 Tips for Replacement:
1.  Replace Both: Since you’re already inside, it’s highly recommended to replace both parts at once. The thermal fuse often blows because of a failing heater (e.g., limescale buildup causing overheating). If you only replace the fuse, the new one might blow again quickly if the heater is still faulty.
2.  Check for Limescale: Before installing the new heater, look inside the drum housing for any thick white crusty limescale. Clean it off with a descaler or vinegar solution to prevent future overheating.
3.  Wiring Diagram: Take photos of your current wiring before you disconnect anything. This will make reassembly much easier and help ensure everything goes back in the correct order.
